strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing catastrophic forgetting in continual learning of MLLMs
Elegant task design using jigsaw puzzles as a genuinely novel task (verified by showing GPT-4o and large models fail)
Key methodological insight isolating data distribution as critical factor through SFT-GRPO-Rollout experiment
Comprehensive empirical evaluation across 4 capability axes with multiple benchmarks showing knowledge retention effects
Compelling quantitative analysis via perplexity (Section 5.4) showing GRPO-generated data better aligns with base model distribution
Novel theoretical perspective via learning dynamics (Theorems 5.1-5.2) with symmetry property explaining forgetting behavior
Clear presentation with informative visualizations and logical experimental flow
weaknesses: Severely limited experimental scope: single model (Qwen2.5-VL-3B only) and single task type (3×3 jigsaw puzzles only)—insufficient for claiming generalizability at top-tier venue
Small test set (100 images) without error bars or significance testing, raising concerns about variance and statistical reliability
Modest absolute performance (66% accuracy on jigsaw puzzles) and no comparison with contemporary work (Jigsaw-R1) in performance progression
No empirical comparison with existing catastrophic forgetting mitigation methods (regularization, memory-replay, architecture-based approaches) despite reviewing them
Learning dynamics theory assumes eNTK stability without empirical validation in this specific setting; first-order approximation validity at reported learning rates not verified
Incomplete ablations: no breakdown of reward components (Rhit, Racc, Rfmt), no hyperparameter sensitivity analysis, no analysis of prompt format confounds between SFT and RFT
Practical complexity: RFT requires periodic restarts to avoid KL divergence explosion; SFT-GRPO-Rollout requires expensive RFT exploration first, limiting practical applicability
Mechanistic gaps: theory explains why low-perplexity data works but not how RFT specifically discovers these regions; why RFT needs 10× more steps than SFT unexplained
Results show performance drops on some benchmarks (DocVQA, GQA) that are dismissed without deeper investigation
Overclaimed findings: title claims 'stably' learning but 66% may not qualify; claims about discovering novel strategies based on single task type

strengths: Addresses an important research question about knowledge retention during post-training of MLLMs
Clever use of jigsaw puzzles as a verified genuinely novel task confirmed to be at ~0% accuracy for SOTA models
Comprehensive empirical evaluation across multiple capability axes (grounding, OCR, VQA, hallucination) with detailed benchmarking
Interesting core finding that SFT on RFT-generated rollouts avoids catastrophic forgetting, suggesting data distribution is critical
Theoretical analysis using learning dynamics framework with novel symmetry property (Theorem 5.2) providing principled perspective
Well-written presentation with clear visualizations and detailed perplexity analysis of data distributions
Thorough ablation studies including varying learning rates showing robustness of findings
weaknesses: Severely limited generalization: single small model (3B parameters) and single task type (3×3 jigsaw puzzles). Findings may not transfer to larger models or diverse novel tasks—critical limitation for top-tier venue
Partially confirmatory of concurrent work (Liu et al., 2025b; Wang et al., 2025; Yue et al., 2025); core observation that RFT reduces forgetting vs. SFT already established

Theoretical analysis relies on unvalidated assumptions (stable eNTK matrix, small learning rates) that may not hold for fine-tuning modern LLMs. Modest perplexity difference (~0.23 vs 0.42) doesn't clearly explain dramatic forgetting disparities in Table 1

Experimental confounds: SFT-GRPO-Rollout uses only ~60% of data (filtered for correctness) mixing data quality with quantity effects; unequal training steps (2,738 for SFT vs 27,360 for GRPO) complicate algorithmic comparison

Practical limitations underexplored: RFT shows training instability requiring periodic restarts (Fig. 6), undermining 'stable learning' claim. Computational cost of RFT-then-SFT pipeline not quantified; limited actionable guidance

No statistical significance testing, error bars, or confidence intervals despite small test set (100 images). No comparison against continual learning baselines (EWC, memory replay) despite literature review mentioning them

Mechanism remains partially speculative: unclear why GRPO's reward signal discovers 'hidden linguistic regions' that manual curation cannot, or whether this is task/model-specific. Missing ablations on reward design sensitivity

Missing reproducibility details: no code/data availability statement, COCO subset selection not fully detailed, number of random seeds unreported. Learning rate ablation (Table 2) changes optimization regime substantially, limiting insights

strengths: Important and well-motivated research question on catastrophic forgetting during fine-tuning, with practical relevance for continual learning
Clever experimental design using jigsaw puzzles as a genuinely novel task (verified as absent from pretraining via GPT-4o and Qwen-72B benchmarking)
Strong isolating experiment (SFT-on-GRPO-Rollout) that convincingly demonstrates data distribution, not algorithm choice, drives forgetting behavior
Comprehensive multi-axis evaluation across grounding, OCR, VQA, and hallucination benchmarks with clear quantitative comparisons
Effective data analysis with clear visualization (Figure 5) showing perplexity distribution differences between GRPO-generated and manually-written data
Learning dynamics theoretical contribution (Theorems 5.1-5.2) providing formal grounding, with elegant symmetry property yielding actionable insights
Well-designed ablation studies including aggressive learning rates (Table 2) and periodic restart analysis (Figure 6)
Generally clear presentation with informative qualitative results and effective visualizations
weaknesses: Limited generality: evaluation restricted to single model (Qwen2.5-VL-3B) and single task (3×3 jigsaw puzzles); lacks evidence that findings generalize to larger models or diverse novel tasks
Insufficient statistical rigor: no error bars, confidence intervals, multiple runs, or significance testing; test set of only 100 images is small

Incomplete analysis of residual forgetting: SFT-GRPO-Rollout still degrades performance on several tasks (e.g., DocVQA -0.25, RefCOCOg -1.34); paper doesn't explain why or characterize task properties that confer robustness
Learning dynamics contribution is incremental: largely applies Ren & Sutherland (2024) framework; key assumption about eNTK stability during MLLM fine-tuning is not empirically validated
Theoretical analysis is post-hoc explanatory rather than predictive; does not prospectively identify when/why forgetting occurs
Confounded experimental design: GRPO data includes chain-of-thought reasoning while SFT-GT does not; unclear if benefits stem from data distribution, reasoning structure, or both
Practical limitations not addressed: GRPO training requires 10× more steps (27,360 vs. 2,738); proposed solution is computationally expensive without clear guidance on when to use it
Perplexity as proxy for alignment is indirect; low perplexity doesn't guarantee meaningful alignment with pretraining intent
Reproducibility concerns: GRPO involves sampling randomness without variance reporting; implementation details on reward weighting and exact prompt format incomplete
Limited scope: no evaluation of alternative RL algorithms, harder puzzle configurations, or diverse task domains; experimental choices lack sensitivity analysis

strengths: Well-motivated research question on catastrophic forgetting in MLLM fine-tuning with clear practical relevance
Clever use of jigsaw puzzles as a genuinely novel task confirmed absent from pretraining (SOTA models fail)
Comprehensive empirical evaluation across two model scales, five capability axes, and multiple data variants with clear performance deltas
Novel actionable finding that SFT on RFT-generated rollouts achieves both good new task performance and better prior knowledge retention
Learning dynamics framework providing interpretable magnitude-direction decomposition of interference via eNTK and perplexity analysis
Multi-perspective analysis combining loss gradients, empirical NTK, perplexity trends, and Pareto front curves for converging evidence
Rigorous theoretical derivations with clear proofs for Theorems 5.1-5.2 and well-presented experimental methodology
weaknesses: Severe generalization limitations: single novel task (jigsaw puzzles) and single model family (Qwen2.5-VL), limiting claims about stable continual learning broadly
Theoretical contributions are incremental—Theorems 5.1-5.2 follow directly from existing learning dynamics theory (Ren & Sutherland 2024) with limited novel insights
Unfair experimental comparison: RFT requires 27,360 steps (7-100× more compute) versus SFT's 200-4,100 steps; computational cost trade-off underexplored
Selection bias in RFT filtering: ~65% of samples are kept based on correctness, which cherry-picks naturally aligned examples without isolating this effect from trajectory format benefits

Critical missing ablations: no comparison of SFT with vs. without reasoning trajectories while controlling for filtering; no sensitivity analysis on reward structure, filtering thresholds, or data size
eNTK stability assumption undervalidated during fine-tuning (distinct from pretraining); LBK bound tightness not empirically assessed; results depend on narrow choice of Grounding as prior knowledge
RFT training instability requiring periodic restarts every 2 epochs (Figure 6), suggesting fragility and reduced practical utility despite theoretical benefits
Perplexity-forgetting link is correlational, not causal; unclear why low PPL is the mechanism rather than confounded with other data properties; lacks intervention experiments

strengths: Addresses important problem of catastrophic forgetting in MLLM fine-tuning with timely relevance
Novel and well-validated task design: jigsaw puzzles (3×3) confirmed absent from pretraining via 0% GPT-4o/Qwen accuracy
Comprehensive prior knowledge evaluation across 5 diverse benchmark axes (Grounding, OCR, VQA, Hallucination, College-level)
Key empirical insight that SFT on RFT-generated rollouts achieves task performance with less forgetting, supporting data-centric hypothesis
Systematic experiments: multiple data variants, two model sizes, hyperparameter variations, Pareto front analysis
Learning dynamics framework provides structured decomposition of interference into magnitude (eNTK) and direction (perplexity)
weaknesses: Single-task generalization: entire analysis restricted to 3×3 jigsaw puzzles; no evidence findings transfer to other novel tasks or complexity levels
Single model family: only Qwen2.5-VL-3B/7B tested; no results on other MLLM architectures (GPT-4V, LLaVA, InternVL, etc.)
Unvalidated theoretical assumptions: eNTK stability assumed but never empirically verified for MLLM fine-tuning; NTK regime assumptions questionable at practical learning rates
Loose theoretical bounds: LBK is lower bound through multiple inequalities; conclusions depend on loose approximations rather than tight analysis
Vision-language gap in theory: eNTK analysis on logit network doesn't account for vision encoder interactions or identify whether forgetting occurs in vision vs. language components
Limited practical actionability: requires expensive RFT (27,360 steps) to generate SFT data, defeating efficiency advantage of SFT; no comparison with cheaper forgetting mitigation strategies
No statistical rigor: single runs on 100 test images, no error bars/confidence intervals, no multiple random seeds, no significance tests
Incomplete analysis of core mechanisms: why RFT generates low-perplexity samples unexplained; why GPT-4o reasoning has high perplexity underexplored
Sample filtering bias: 65% threshold for successful rollouts lacks justification and sensitivity analysis; filtering criteria incompletely specified
Missing critical comparisons: no comparison with other catastrophic forgetting mitigation methods (EWC, replay, adapters); limited engagement with concurrent RL's Razor work
Prior knowledge representation limited: only Grounding task used as proxy; may not represent diverse knowledge types
Overstated claims: paper argues general principles about RFT vs SFT despite evidence limited to one task on one model family
Missing ablations: reasoning trajectory length, reward component importance (Rhit/Racc/Rfmt), sensitivity to filtering threshold
Unverified perplexity mechanism: unclear why base model perplexity should specifically correlate with preserving downstream task performance

strengths: Important practical problem addressing catastrophic forgetting in MLLMs during post-training, with high relevance for deployment
Clever use of jigsaw puzzles as genuinely novel task (verified with GPT-4o failure), providing fair testbed for studying knowledge retention
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple benchmarks (Grounding, OCR, General VQA, Hallucination, MMMU) with consistent trends and clear ablations
Key insight isolating data distribution as primary factor over algorithmic differences, demonstrated via SFT-Rea-GRPO-Rollout experiments
Principled theoretical framework using learning dynamics to decompose forgetting into magnitude and direction, with elegant symmetry result (Theorem 5.2)
Practical utility: showing RFT-generated rollouts enable SFT to match RFT performance while reducing forgetting provides actionable guidance
Well-written with clear presentation, good visualizations, honest discussion of limitations, and commitment to open-sourcing code
weaknesses: Limited novelty of core finding: RFT reducing catastrophic forgetting already documented in concurrent work (Liu et al. 2025b, Wang et al. 2025); primary contribution is explanation via learning dynamics framework built heavily on existing work (Ren & Sutherland 2024)

Significant scope limitations severely restricting generalizability: only single novel task (jigsaw puzzles, spatial reasoning), only one model family (Qwen2.5-VL 3B/7B), no experiments on other architectures despite acknowledged importance

Theoretical analysis makes strong assumptions: eNTK stability assumption is non-trivial in post-training regime; LBK provides only lower bound with unclear tightness; O(η²) error terms could be significant but sensitivity not analyzed

Experimental design issues: inconsistent training steps across methods (SFT: 200-4,100 vs RFT: 27,360) complicates comparison; filtering threshold (65% correctness) for RFT rollouts not ablated; prior knowledge (Grounding tasks) selection appears arbitrary
Insufficient practical analysis of computational trade-offs: RFT requires ~137× more steps than SFT; mentioned lightweight alternative underdeveloped; operating point selection guidance missing

Incomplete analysis of mechanism: circular reasoning risk in using perplexity to explain perplexity effects; limited discussion of when RFT fails or high-perplexity data could be valuable; reward signal sensitivity unexplored

Missing comparisons and ablations: no comparison with other catastrophic forgetting mitigation strategies (EWC, adapter methods); no sensitivity analysis for RFT filtering threshold; task similarity analysis absent

strengths: Comprehensive and well-designed experiments across multiple domains (jigsaw puzzles, math reasoning, scientific QA) with multiple model scales and extensive benchmarks for prior knowledge evaluation
Novel use of jigsaw puzzles as a genuinely new task (verified 0% accuracy on SOTA models) provides a clean testbed for studying catastrophic forgetting
Insightful learning dynamics framework (Theorems 5.1-5.2) that decomposes forgetting into magnitude and direction, with elegant symmetry property explaining low-perplexity training benefits

Strong empirical finding that SFT on RFT-generated rollouts achieves comparable task performance to RFT while reducing forgetting, providing compelling evidence that data distribution is the critical factor
Excellent reproducibility with detailed hyperparameters, algorithm descriptions, extensive appendix, and promise to open-source code
Clear presentation with informative figures and comprehensive tables demonstrating consistent patterns across different settings
weaknesses: Limited novelty of core insight: RFT's benefits for catastrophic forgetting mitigation are known from concurrent work (Jigsaw-R1, RL's Razor); main contribution (data-centric explanation) is somewhat intuitive

Strong theoretical assumptions only partially validated: eNTK stability assumption validated for pretraining, not post-training; relative influence stability assumption unvalidated for this setting; LBK is an approximation whose tightness is unknown
Narrow model scope: only Qwen2.5 family tested (3B, 7B); no experiments on other architectures (Llama, GPT variants) or larger models (13B+), limiting generalization claims
Limited task scope for MLLMs: only 3×3 jigsaw puzzles despite paper claiming general insights; would benefit from additional novel visual tasks to validate generalization

Insufficient ablations on confounding factors: reasoning trajectories could improve beyond perplexity alignment (intermediate supervision); mixture experiments show mixing doesn't help but more systematic ablations needed (high-PPL reasoning data, low-PPL non-reasoning data)
Computational cost trade-offs underexplored: RFT requires ~550x more GPU-hours than SFT (2200 vs 4 GPU-hours); practical scenarios often prefer speed, deserving more discussion
Statistical rigor issues: no error bars, confidence intervals, or significance testing; single test set (100 images); multiple comparisons without correction
Perplexity-centric analysis has limitations: high PPL doesn't necessarily imply harm; perplexity is model-specific; using it as main metric is somewhat crude despite theoretical justification

Key experimental design choices need better justification: filtering RFT data to 65% introduces selection bias; varying training steps across conditions (Table 1) complicates comparisons; GRPO periodic restarts add complexity

Generalization questions unaddressed: applicability to tasks far from pretraining distribution unclear; unclear if findings hold for larger models or different model families; limited discussion of when framework breaks down

strengths: Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple model sizes and diverse benchmarks (grounding, OCR, VQA, hallucination, math reasoning, science QA)
Well-motivated task design using jigsaw puzzles as a genuinely novel task with confirmed zero baseline accuracy
Clear empirical demonstration that RFT-generated data reduces catastrophic forgetting better than externally-generated reasoning trajectories
Extensive ablations, controls, and reproducibility details including hyperparameters and promise to release code
Useful practical finding that SFT on RFT-rollouts can match RFT performance while reducing forgetting
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: the core insight that 'data distribution matters' is intuitive and predictable; the finding reduces to 'RFT data has lower perplexity because it comes from model distribution'

Weak theoretical contributions: Theorems 5.1-5.2 are straightforward applications of first-order Taylor expansions and matrix algebra, not novel. The connection between eNTK magnitude and low-perplexity preventing forgetting is asserted but not rigorously derived

Circular reasoning in explanation: the paper demonstrates RFT-generated data has low perplexity (expected, since RFT generates high-probability sequences) but doesn't mechanistically explain WHY low perplexity prevents forgetting

Narrow experimental scope for MLLMs: only one novel task type (jigsaw puzzles) evaluated; generalization to other task types unclear. All prior benchmarks share similar output formats (closed answers, bounding boxes)

Unclear practical impact: SFT-Rea-GRPO-Rollout still requires 5,472 RFT steps plus SFT steps (~8 GPU-hours total), not substantially cheaper than RFT. The recommended approach adds complexity without clear advantage
Limited analysis of confounds: Rea-GRPO vs Rea-4o data differ in perplexity, reasoning quality, and source; not cleanly isolated which factor matters most
eNTK analysis uses a Lower Bound approximation with unknown tightness; stability assumption for eNTK not thoroughly validated empirically

Perplexity serves as proxy but not justified as the right metric: Figure 4 shows substantial overlap between distributions; no explanation of why low perplexity fundamentally prevents forgetting rather than merely correlating
Small model sizes (3B, 7B only): unclear if findings generalize to 70B+ where different forgetting dynamics might emerge
Generalization concerns: artificial task (jigsaw puzzles); extensions to math/science still focus on reasoning tasks with limited diversity; only Qwen models tested

strengths: Comprehensive empirical validation across multiple domains (MLLMs on vision, LLMs on math, science QA) with proper experimental controls and ablations
Novel theoretical perspective using learning dynamics framework (Theorems 5.1-5.2) that elegantly decomposes interference into magnitude and direction, with insightful symmetry property
Well-motivated experimental design with jigsaw puzzles as genuinely novel task (zero-shot performance confirms novelty), enabling fair evaluation of SFT vs. RFT
Key practical insight that data distribution rather than algorithm drives forgetting; demonstrated via SFT-Rea-GRPO-Rollout achieving RFT performance with better prior knowledge retention
Strong empirical support across 5 capability axes with thorough ablations (learning rates, GRPO recipes, mixture approaches), good statistical rigor
Clear actionable findings with practical implications (brief RFT can generate stable training data) and analysis of SFT-RFT cooperation
Excellent reproducibility with detailed hyperparameters, extensive appendices, and promised code release
weaknesses: Core observation that RFT mitigates catastrophic forgetting has been shown in concurrent work (Lai et al. 2025; Wang et al. 2025; Shenfeld et al. 2025); this paper provides incremental empirical validation and theoretical analysis rather than novel discovery

Learning dynamics framework relies on eNTK stability assumption borrowed from prior work with limited empirical validation in post-training setting; practical validity unclear given potential significant distribution shifts during fine-tuning
Lower bound kernel (Eq. 7) may be quite loose, limiting predictive utility; framework primarily serves post-hoc explanation rather than enabling new algorithmic innovations

Mechanistic understanding has circularity: RFT samples are low-perplexity by construction (sampled from base), paper shows low-PPL→less forgetting, but causal mechanism (why low-perplexity intrinsically reduces interference) not deeply explained beyond symmetry argument

Multimodal experiments limited to single novel task (jigsaw puzzles); claims about generalizability would be stronger with multiple distinct vision-language tasks (counting, novel objects, spatial reasoning, etc.)
Limited model diversity for MLLMs (only Qwen2.5-VL); findings' generalizability to other architectures (LLaVA, GPT-4V, Claude) unclear

Incomplete practical guidance: 10x computational difference (27,360 vs. 2,670 steps) not fully analyzed; when should practitioners use which approach? Section 5.8 partially addresses but lacks comprehensive trade-off analysis

Missing comparisons to classical continual learning baselines (EWC, SI, rehearsal with pretraining data); alternative approaches to achieve similar benefits underexplored beyond brief mixture experiments
